The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

If a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) has handled impure food with unclean hands—meaning he previously grasped food that was defiled by a monk—and then distributes roasted grain or cooked rice to the Saṃgha, the single person who is the presiding elder (*sthavira*) receives what is impure, while those of the other names receive what is pure.
If a pure person holds pure flour and pours it onto impure flour, one may take what has been poured on top;
however, if impure flour is poured onto pure flour, all of it becomes impure.
If pure flour is placed within an impure vessel, one may scoop out the center;
however, if the basket or vessel has been shaken, everything is impure.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
If impure food is mixed within pure food, one should remove and discard that which must be discarded and eat the remainder.
The same principle applies to cakes, fruits, and so forth. Regarding various types of grains, they may be distinguished by their appearance;
however, if the characteristics of purity and impurity are indistinguishable, then all of it should be replaced.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
When drying grain, if a bhikṣu walks upon it, he should have a lay attendant (*karmadāna*) clear away the area where his feet tread;
however, if there is an urgent matter or difficulty, there is no offense even if he treads upon it.

If it rains and there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), one may personally cast a clean mat or object from afar over the food to cover it, and hold a clean brick or stone to weigh it down.
The same applies if one forgets to cover the food vessels.

If, within a kitchen, there are various jars of ghee and oil, bundles of sugarcane, bamboo, or reeds, and a bhikṣu takes a jar of oil or honey for the seven-day period but mistakenly grasps a jar of pure oil;
if another person sees this, they must not speak immediately, but wait until he asks them, "What kind of oil is this? [only then may they inform him].
The answer is: "Seven-day oil.

One should tell [the layperson] to place it on the ground; since no specific name is required, one may receive it for seven days even if it was brought by mistake due to a handling error, as such an error does not invalidate the act.

If one instructs them to bring pure oil, and the layperson, not understanding, brings seven-day oil by mistake, one should follow the aforementioned method; however, there is a fault according to the oral tradition.
The same applies to other instances of grasping incorrectly.
If one says, "Be careful!
Look at the ash-pitcher and bring it here!"
This bhikṣu reached his hand into the jar and mistakenly grasped pure flour while looking at it; therefore, it was called "pure.
If he had returned it to the jar, it would have been considered "impure. The remaining cases should be treated according to this analogy.
Regarding "clear contact within a vessel": all leaf-wrappings constitute a vessel, whereas those that are unfolded do not.
A vessel consists of a basin with its rim submerged in parched barley.
Long benches, sitting benches, rope beds, and finely woven mats constitute vessels.
When a boat is on the water or when a carriage startles an ox, these are not suitable vessels;
rather, that which is empty serves as the vessel.

At mealtime, one may arrange long boards, benches, or mattresses upon sugar cane, radishes, bags of rice, grains, or beans, and have the bhikṣu sit there; he should not move his body, nor should he ask questions.
If the object being moved is questioned [as to its purity], all that is impure becomes permissible to sit upon due to the presence of a supporting condition;

however, if it is moved and touched, it constitutes a transgression. If, on a loft or a clothes rack, there is pure food, robes, or a bowl, and one takes an object while moving the pure vessel or food, everything becomes impure;
if the loft is solid and does not move, it is permissible.
If one is on a boat carrying seventeen kinds of grain, covered with mats of *qúchú* grass, a bhikṣu may sit upon it without violating the precept;
however, if it is driven by the wind or swirling waves and drifts onto the shore, it becomes entirely impure.
Only if the ropes and oars do not leave the water is it considered pure.
If a large cart is loaded with various grains and covered over, a bhikṣu may sit upon it, provided he does not touch the grain; this is like being on a boat while traveling.
If there is pure substance in a small cart, and if the cart is moved when taking up robes or bowls, everything becomes impure.
One must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) take them; one must not, because of the presence of an ox, regard it as sexual misconduct.
One should have the *karmadāna* (lay attendant) board first, with the bhikṣu boarding afterwards;
when descending, the bhikṣu should descend first.
If they are on a cart loaded with goods and it suddenly overturns and separates from the oxen, everything becomes impure.
If the ox’s rope has not yet been detached from the cart, it is called "pure.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

If a bhikṣu and a śrāmaṇera are carrying food along a road, and at the time of eating the bhikṣu gives it to the śrāmaṇera, who then returns it to the bhikṣu—if they did not previously make an agreement [to exchange], he may eat it.
The opposite of this is not permitted.

If a śrāmaṇera carries food while crossing water and there is fear that one might drown, one may even carry it on one's own shoulder; although there is no offense in holding it, one must not hold onto it once they reach the shore.

If one receives flour in an impure vessel, one should not discard it all; rather, that which adheres to the bowl should be discarded, while the remainder may be eaten, as is the case in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
If, while receiving hot gruel with a bowl fastened by a cord, fat oozes out from within, one should simply discard the fat where it falls;
the remainder may be eaten.
If the vessels for rice, gruel, or soup tip over, it is permitted to have an attendant adjust them, but once they are upright, one must not touch them again.
If one assists in supporting a clean cauldron, it is the same.
If a lay attendant tips over a jar of ghee or oil, it is the same.
If a person, donkey, ox, or cart carrying food tips over, it is also the same.

When the wind, rain, or weather are favorable, if clean vessels are left empty in the open air, one should wash one's hands thoroughly, lift them up, and place them in a covered location; this is "purity by nature" (*tǐjìng*).
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:

if there is no pure attendant (*śuci-pudgala*) and a vessel for ghee or oil is not covered, one may personally grasp the lid and suspend it over the vessel; this is called "purity by circumstance" (*yuànjìng*).
If a layperson entrusts food to a bhikṣu for safekeeping, and later requests it back to give to that bhikṣu, he may receive it after washing his hands.
If food has entered the holes or cavities of a bowl, he may wash those parts that can be cleaned; as for the remainder that cannot be removed, there is no offense.

If one enters the midst of the Saṃgha for a meal and lacks a bowl, it is permitted to borrow one from a neighboring seat or from anyone within the Saṃgha who has one; this is also considered *tīrtha-śuddhi* (pure by nature).
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"When a bhikṣu blows air into a vessel intended for purification, it is called 'defiled' (*spṛṣṭa*)."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
If the oil-jar suddenly overturns, one should right it oneself without letting it leave the ground.
If a wicked person throws a handful of impure rice into pure rice, that which can be separated should be removed.
Regarding that which cannot be divided, take a handful and depart.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"If one scatters seeds oneself and they grow into vegetables, it is permitted to eat them."
If one moves vegetables to plant them so that they may grow again, it is likewise permissible for other fruits and vegetables by analogy.
If a novice (śrāmaṇera) is small and carries pure food across water, it is permitted for a bhikṣu to support him;
if he is climbing an embankment, he may also be supported.
If one lifts up pure food that is suspended, one must place it upon a bed, a small table, a stool, or the like, so that it may be lowered down.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If a person carrying pure food takes it from above, and a *mahābhikṣu* touches the food with his own hand, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
When one is ill and takes medicine that may cause transgression, one should do so in a secluded place where others cannot see.
The *Vinaya* states: "If one obtains rice to provide for guests, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a 'pure person') receive it."
Second, regarding cooking for oneself:
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If the *kappiya-kāraka* (the person who prepares what is allowable) is ill at the place of practice, or if there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, once pure grain has been obtained, the bhikṣu may husk it himself and make gruel to give to the *kappiya-kāraka*."

If the *karmadāna* (lay attendant) has not finished eating, one must not eat it oneself; however, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if there was no prior intention to share [the food] but one gives it with a single-minded resolve, it is also permissible.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

If a lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) is difficult to find and a bhikṣu wishes to prepare food himself, he should personally wash a vessel that has not been contaminated by grease, fill it with water, and naturally ignite a fire to bring it to a boil; this constitutes "purity by nature" (*prakṛti-śuddhi*).
If the monastic utensils are greasy, it is improper to ignite them with fire; one must be cautioned against this.
After having a *kappiyakāraka* (a lay attendant) place [the food] into boiling water within the vessel, the monk must not touch it again.

Once the *kappiyakāraka* has brought it to a boil, the monk may place a piece of wood horizontally across the ground and stand upon it. He then instructs the *kappiyakāraka* to place the cooking vessel upon the wood. The monk then says, "I receive, I receive," and subsequently cooks it himself until it is done before giving it to the sick person. He must ensure that no unaccepted object falls into the food.
Even boiling vegetables until they wither follows the same procedure as above.
One must not boil ginger decoction oneself, as it would change from raw to cooked.
However, if one obtains cold food by begging and warms or boils it oneself, there is no offense.
When preparing food, a young attendant may be allowed to hold one's hand while being instructed to rinse, pour, or ladle out the rice.
Regarding the third point, "storing overnight within," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
If a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to prepare food) has not finished washing vegetables on impure ground when the dawn light appears, there is no offense.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is stated that if a bhikṣu brings food and, unable to find pure ground, the dawn light appears before he can do so, there is no offense.
Regarding "cooking within the four boundaries":
if one is inside the boundary and the food was originally cooked for others rather than being prepared solely for oneself,
and if there is a surplus from which others may partake, one should wash one's hands and receive the food.
The section on the three clarifications regarding permissibility and prohibition is divided into two parts.
First, regarding the four types of medicinal substances:
if it is a "timely medicine" (*kālabhojana*), it must necessarily have been boiled overnight.
Because they are strengthening substances that must be consumed regularly, one drinks them.
Regarding the three medicines that do not undergo the formal ritual (*kalpa*), there is first the "simultaneous medicine" (*sāmayika-bhaiṣajya*);
if they are added through a sacred ritual for the sake of a specific illness, then there is both general and restricted application.
Regarding post-midday medicine (*akālabhaiṣajya*): it may be consumed at any time before the appearance of the morning light after midday has passed;

however, once the morning light appears, its status as "oral medicine" (*mukhavaḍika*) is lost, and it becomes subject to the faults of being stored overnight (*śeṣabhakta*), having been touched by impurity (*duṣṭasparśa*), or being taken at an improper time (*akāla*).

Regarding the seven-day medicine: once the ritual procedure has been performed and it has been placed within the inner clean kitchen, it is permitted to be kept without the faults of "remaining overnight" or "improper handling.
When one rises on the morning of the eighth day, the offenses incurred are as described below.

"Throughout one's life" refers necessarily to that which is fully ripened and dead, lacking the characteristics of a seed capable of growth; the Vinaya permits keeping food overnight, cooking indoors, and cooking for oneself.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that cooking ginger soup for oneself constitutes an offense; by this principle, anything possessing the potential for growth is likewise included, and thus three offenses are permitted under these conditions.
"One must not stay overnight for seven days.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Honey syrup may be kept overnight; it is permitted for a sick person to drink it, as this constitutes a difficult circumstance."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Regarding leftover ghee or oil kept overnight, it is permitted for use such as nasal irrigation.
Other impure medicines do not permit the addition of ritual mantras; this is the authentic text of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*."
Second, the four faults are explained.
First, the characteristics of the faults are clarified:
namely, storing indoors, cooking indoors, cooking for oneself, and improper contact.

Regarding the beginning and middle [of this matter], the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are three types of persons who may consume food overnight: individual bhikṣus, the Saṃgha, and śrāmaṇeras undergoing penance; these are termed "overnight storage within" (*naiḥsargika-pācattika*).
Among the nuns, there are four types; three are as described above, with the addition of the *śikṣamāṇā*.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:

a *śikṣamāṇā* may receive food from a fully ordained nun (*bhikṣuṇī*) after the meal has ended, but she must not sleep together with her; this is permitted because there were no *śrāmaṇerīs* [at that time].

"Storing within" refers to eating and sleeping together with others inside a monastic dwelling after it has been designated as a pure area (*pariśuddha-sthāna*), without ever having stated that there is a monk present in that pure area.
"Cooking within" refers to boiling food inside a monastic dwelling after it has been designated as a pure area.
Regarding "cooked by oneself": if a great bhikṣu prepares it himself, it should not be eaten by the three types of persons mentioned above.

Regarding "badly grasped": having personally taken fruit and given it to one who has performed the purification ritual, if one receives it back again to eat it, this is a case of "indeterminate relinquishment"; giving it to another and then receiving it back is likewise considered "badly grasped."
*The Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*: Regarding eating together with overnight-stored food, there are three cases:

having received the food and formed the thought that it belongs to oneself, whether one stays overnight with it or not; if one stays through the night, it is a *duṣkṛta* (transgression), and if one eats it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), because it is "leftover overnight" food.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is the same in this regard.
If one takes food with one's own hand, it is called "improper grasping"; if one forms the thought that it belongs to oneself and lets it remain overnight, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one eats food that has neither been formally received nor grasped, yet directly forms the thought that it belongs to oneself and lets it remain overnight, eating it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If others have eaten it, there is no fault in consuming it after it has been kept overnight.
These two [points] take these four faults as their basis, clarifying them by way of time, place, and food.

Regarding the initial practice of "storing within" (*antar-śayana*): as for that which pertains to the specific location, it does not apply to other objects, nor does it apply to the two types of purification;
however, it applies universally to the demarcation of the site, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and that which is within the boundary (*sīmā*).
Regarding the time, it must be during the period when the dawn light appears.
Regarding the person, it refers specifically to three bhikṣus who know that [the offense] exists; such is the transgression.
In the Vinaya, it asks:
Regarding the case where the pure ground has not yet reached the appearance of dawn, a dog brings food, or the wind blows fruit down:
the Vinaya states that if one does not know [of these occurrences], there is no offense.
For a nun, it is an offense when four people are present, as described above.
Regarding the consumption of food: if the object has been lifted off the ground, all [types of food] constitute an offense;
if it has not been lifted off the ground, or if it has not yet grown legs (i.e., sprouted), there is no offense.
That they have already grown tall, encountered frost, and so forth, are all matters of past karmic destiny;
the discussion regarding the four medicines is as above.
Second, "cooking within" refers to:
Regarding the location, it must be on clean ground and the area must be enclosed.
Regarding the time, it may be during the day or night.
Regarding the persons involved, it applies to all seven classes of followers.
Regarding the "approximate food" (*yuktaka-bhojana*), it includes both raw and cooked varieties;

however, in terms of the four medicines, only those for which the ritual addition (*adhivāsana*) has been performed and which are permitted to be kept overnight within the boundary (*sīmā*) and cooked throughout one's life are allowed,
because the other three do not conform to these conditions.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Ānanda was warming the Buddha’s rice near the gate of the Jetavana.
From this, we know that one must not cook within the boundary (*sīmā*)."
Regarding the third, "cooking for oneself":
as for the location, it applies to both pure and impure grounds;
as for the time, it applies to both day and night.
Regarding the persons involved, there are three members of the great *saṃgha* and four among the nuns.
Regarding the production of food, since the Buddha permitted re-cooking, there is no offense;
among the four medicines, the addition of the formula for life-long use is likewise permitted.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If it is raw food, once it has been purified by fire, it may be cooked.
How is it purified?"
This applies by analogy to cases such as fire touching [food] even once, or the example of warming cold food with vegetables and the like.
In the *Five Hundred Questions*:
"If it has been treated with pure medicinal herbs, a bhikṣu may prepare it himself."
There are four types of unwholesome contact:
in terms of location, they pertain to both pure and impure grounds;
in terms of time, they pertain to both day and night.
Regarding those who approach [the Sangha], there are several types of *mahāsangha* (great monks):
first, those who initially refuse [an offering] but then directly seize and touch it;
second, those whose oily residues remain connected [to others], like robes, bowls, or cloths that have not been washed clean and thus become defiled by mutual contact.

Third, regarding the loss of the formal undertaking (*samādāna*) through spontaneous occurrence and the four methods of non-administration of medicine: in the case of the middle and subsequent [medicines], the undertaking is lost at both times;
if the method of administration is applied, the undertaking for each of the three medicines is lost immediately upon reaching its respective limit;
fourth, the loss of the undertaking due to encountering conditions refers to the touching of the bed or utensils by a lay attendant (*upasthāyaka*).
The fifth case of intentional relinquishment through loss is like having accepted food and then not eating it;
later, when one needs it, one takes it without having formally received it again, thereby incurring a *pācittiya* offense.

If one approaches a *śrāmaṇera* or a *kappiya-kāraka*, and there is contact with oily residue—meaning that after grasping a bhikṣu’s bowl, oil remains on the hand, and one grasps a monastic utensil without washing it.
Furthermore, there are four types of non-offensive contact for the great *saṃgha*:

first, receiving by grasping as one would with a secular vessel; for instance, when food is placed in a vessel held by a layperson and given to a *bhikṣu*, who receives it with an upturned hand—although both the monastic and the layperson previously grasped the food, no offensive contact is incurred.

The same applies to food already in the bowl: there are two ways it loses its status as "received" (paribhukta) or becomes "touched by a non-purifier" (aśuci-puruṣa-sparśita). First, if one touches it while washing hands, one must receive it again from the purifier; the purifier does not need to wash their hands. Second, if one who observes the precepts mistakenly grasps it, or if one who has broken the precepts intentionally touches it, both are termed "pure food."
Furthermore, they are distinguished by three phrases:
first, "touching but not evil.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
Regarding a precept-observing bhikṣu who inadvertently touches monastic food:
according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*,
if one forgets to receive [the food] by hand and carries it while walking, upon seeing a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant), one should place it on the ground, wash one's hands, and receive it again.
The second [type] is improper contact.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts intentionally touching [a woman] is called 'pure'."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
Because various bhikṣus harbored mutual resentment, they touched others' pure food, causing it to become impure;
the Buddha said:
"Not touching is pure; touching is impure, constituting a *duṣkṛta* offense.
In all three cases, touching is also evil.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
When a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts touches [fruit] out of negligence, it is called impure contact (*aśuddha-sparśa*).
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, picking fruit from a tree to test whether it is ripe or raw is also termed evil contact (*duṣṭa-sparśa*).
Regarding food, it includes both raw and cooked varieties.
As for the mutual concealment of offenses leading to expulsion mentioned in the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya): [it states as follows:]

If food items are placed upon a tree and all are severed from the root—if the tree's roots are in impure ground while the branches and leaves cover pure ground, and the fruit falls onto pure ground; or if it is blown by the wind, struck by rain, or dropped by birds or beasts;

provided that no person touches or knows of it, and it falls due to such circumstances—even if it passes through the "bright phase" (the dawn), it does not constitute "overnight storage" (*antarvasa*), which is termed "fruit with long legs."

If fruits or vegetables from impure ground have not yet fully grown but sprout repeatedly as they are moved about, there is no fault of "storing overnight"; they may be gathered at any time and brought into the pure kitchen.

If fruits or vegetables have already been removed from their original location, they may not be eaten by a bhikṣu once the dawn has appeared, provided he is aware of this; the preceding meaning is based on the Vinaya text, which is not explicit.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If the roots of a tree are situated on pure ground while the trunk is on impure ground—or if the roots are on impure ground while the trunk is on pure ground—and a monk is likewise situated on pure ground while the trunk is on impure ground;
if fruit falls therein, it is not the doing of the monk, and he may eat it after it has remained overnight."

If one sees that fruit has fallen onto ground that is not pure, and causes a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food) to gather it up, then after it has remained overnight, if one cannot distinguish whether the location is pure or impure, eating it is permitted;
however, if one knows it is on impure ground, it must not be eaten.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
If a tree stands on pure ground and its fruit falls onto impure ground, it may be gathered at any time;
however, if fruit from either pure or impure ground falls onto impure ground, it must be placed inside the clean kitchen immediately.
If melons or gourds grow in an impure place, they should be picked at the proper time and brought inside a clean house.
The same principle applies to the transporting of grain, rice, beans, and so forth.
In all these cases, if the bhikṣu was unaware that the items were in an impure place, they become pure.
If one knows [the cloth is] impure, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that knowing or not knowing the cloth is largely the same as this rule.
Regarding the fifth point, the period of scarcity permitted eight matters.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says:

Because grain and rice became extremely scarce and prices soared, the people suffered from famine and it was difficult to obtain alms; even when a small amount of food was obtained, it was seized by bandits.

Out of compassion, the Buddha permitted the following within the boundaries of the monastery: eating together with those who reside within the boundary, cooking within the boundary, cooking for oneself, and taking food for oneself;
furthermore, both monastic and lay food, as well as fruits from both water and land, did not require the ritual of *kṛtānna* (the formal declaration of surplus food).
If one were to determine the offenses, eight transgressions should be distinguished:

eating indoors, cooking indoors, cooking for oneself, improper contact with food, eating what has not been formally received, eating after having finished a meal, and the three *pāyattika* rules concerning leftover food kept overnight;

furthermore, there are four *dukkaṭa* (or *duṣkṛta*) offenses, to which the principle of destroying living beings is added—for instance, if one eats the fruit of water or land plants without having formally received it, how could that possibly be considered pure?
The Vinaya states:
"If at a time when the world has fallen into decline, one relies on the allowance to eat;
the Buddha said this is not permitted, and one must be dealt with according to the law."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"In times of famine, after one has finished eating, one may take the leftovers away, provided one informs the donor.
This concludes the fourth major section: the rules for purifying cultivated seeds.
Within this, there are three parts:
namely, the intention for the regulation, the persons involved, and the pure dharma.
Regarding the intention for the regulation, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Vyākhyā-prakaraṇa-śāstra* state:

Various laypeople and non-Buddhists claim that all grasses and trees possess life-force (*jīvitendriya*); because the Buddha did not establish a precept against this, when a bhikṣu harms grasses or trees, he is rebuked by others and causes them to incur guilt;
furthermore, such conduct is no different from that of a white-robed layperson, which fails to engender a mind of reverence.
Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* refers to this as "the rapid extinction of the True Dharma" and further prescribes restrictive regulations.
The rest is as explained in the section on the precept against destroying living beings.
Second, the clarification of the person [to whom it applies].
If a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to perform the purification) performs the purification, there are four cases:
1. If both the person and the fruit are in a pure area (*kappiyabhūmi*), the purification is accomplished; this is most excellent. 2.

If both the person and the fruit are in an impure area (*akappiyabhūmi*), the purification is accomplished, yet it is not permissible to eat [the fruit] because it was ripened within [the impure area]; the remaining four classes of the community may eat it.
The remaining two phrases are from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*; thus the text says:
"If the fruit is on impure ground, one who is pure may perform the purification by means of fire or a knife on that which is on pure ground; although it becomes purified, it may not be eaten."
If the fruit is in a pure area, and one who is pure performs the purification rite in an impure area, it is termed "purified" and may be eaten.
This is the third method of purification.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
At every mealtime, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should ask: "Are the fruits and vegetables pure?
Are they free of insects?
The questioning and answering should be performed according to the Dharma.
The same applies to the *karmadāna*.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are ten types [of pure meat]:
the first five are fire-purified, knife-purified, wound-purified, pecked-by-bird-purified, and unfit-for-seeding-purified.
Among these five types, those that have been wounded by a blade or purified by birds may be eaten after removing the seeds;
those that cannot be planted or purified by fire may be eaten entirely.
As for the next five types—whether their bark has been stripped, their skin peeled, or they are rotten, cracked, or withered—they should be considered pure root-seeds.
It is further stated:
"Washing root vegetables with water constitutes purification; this accords with the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* regarding the purification of root-propagated seeds.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is said that coriander, *śigru*, *jīvañjīvaka*, and other such plants are purified by crushing them.
Regarding those sown from stems, they are purified by removing the eyes;
regarding the seventeen kinds of grain, they are purified by stripping away the husks; regarding those sown from encased seeds, such as melons, they are purified by cleaning the rind.
Fruits of the *phalgu* variety are purified by fire;
fruits of the *śāli* variety are likewise purified by fire;
and fruits of the *tuṣa* variety—if they have not yet had their seeds rubbed out—are purified by fire, provided they possess seeds.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Fire-purification applies to five types.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
"Cleaning by water and cleaning by dusting are signs that [the fruit] should be destroyed.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If many fruits are in the same vessel, once one fruit has been purified, the others may all be used."
If they are separate vessels, each one must be purified individually.
For sugarcane placed upon leaves, each stalk must be purified;
if there are none, the bundle as a whole is purified. By this same principle, for types such as mugwort grass where seeds or fruit have fallen onto it, there is no method for purification.
If it concerns non-glutinous rice, this refers to cases where, after being beaten with a staff and the outer husks removed, there remains a white inner skin; if planted, it can still sprout.

Or, as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when a bhikṣu prepares food and first purifies items such as radish roots by means of fire-purification (*tejodhātu-pariśuddhi*) or knife-purification (*śastra-pariśuddhi*), if they are set aside unused and then sprout again, they must be purified once more.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:

A bhikṣu should not perform the purification rite (*pariśuddhi*) himself; he should place the object on the ground and have a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) perform it. Having washed his hands, he should receive it again in the presence of another person.
If no such person is present, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Vyākhyā-śāstra*) says:
Regarding "performed by oneself during the preparatory stage," the *Śāstra* explains:
this does not mean that one may perform the purification oneself; however, performing it oneself is beneficial.
It is like a cluster of fruit: if it has not been purified, eating only the skin and flesh constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for each instance;
if one eats the seeds, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for each instance.

Now, by a single touch with fire, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense while causing an entire heap of fruit to become pure; since this spares one from many transgressions, how could this not be beneficial?
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* asks:
"What is purification by fire?
It is even as much as a single touch with fire."
If it is purified by means of flames, hot ashes, charcoal, or the like, it does not constitute purification.
When a bhikṣu purifies it himself, other bhikṣus should not eat it; however, that which has been touched by fire may be eaten if it has been further purified by a knife or fingernails.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"The two types, roots and stalks, are purified by fire.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
If tree fruit has been burned by a forest fire and the pile of grain is surrounded by ashes, it is considered pure even if there is fear that non-humans might have stolen it.
If one eats the seeds of such fruit, they are permitted for consumption once they have been purified by fire.

If the husk is purified but not by fire, and one eats the kernel, it is a *pācittiya* offense; this constitutes a "defiled characteristic" (*bhedaka-lakṣaṇa*), though the seed itself is not destroyed.
If it is purified by fire but not by removing the husk, both may be eaten.
If neither the husk nor the kernel is purified, there is one *pācittiya* and one *duṣkṛta*.
Both [methods] are unoffensive when performed.
However, the single method of purification by fire applies to both seeds and characteristics.
The remainder is as explained in the *Anuvyañjana* (Chapter on Characteristics).

*Vyākhyā-śāstra*: This purified dharma is not established merely with respect to a single object. For example, in a cluster of peaches and plums, if fire touches only one, all the others become purified;
likewise, if it is cut by a knife or injured by a claw, whichever one is purified, all the rest are designated as purified.
This constitutes the essence of purification; it takes this as its fundamental method rather than seeking to prevent the growth of things, and is therefore called "śramaṇa-purification" (saṃlekha).
Just as there is grain within rice, it is like the aforementioned purification by removing the husk; other practices are to be understood accordingly.
Question:
What is the distinction between the seed (bīja) and the characteristic (lakṣaṇa)? Answer:

Regarding "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa): this refers to all fruits and vegetables that have white hairs upon them, yet remain green in their original state without changing color, possessing characteristics identical to those growing from the ground;
as the Vinaya states, these are the "seven kinds of colors" found in plants and trees.
What is called "seed" refers to that which can be planted;
it includes those species that, even when separated from the earth, are capable of growing through conditions.
The Vinaya states that there are five kinds of roots.
This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Following Characteristics" (*Anulakṣaṇa*). Fifth, regarding the differences in the methods of undertaking the precepts:

the two types of undertaking—by hand and by mouth—are used daily and constantly; if these were not explained extensively, the characteristics of the teachings would be difficult to manifest. Therefore, taking only the essential matters, they are organized into eight sections:

1. The two types of formal authorization (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*); 2. The two authorizations apply to all four medicinal substances; 3. The third [section] concerns differences regarding the persons addressed; 4. The fourth concerns distinctions in the application of ritual procedures (*adhikāra*); 5. The fifth concerns the scope of the "purification through declaration" (*śuddhi-uddeśa*); 6. The sixth concerns the breadth or narrowness of the two authorizations; 7. The seventh concerns whether subsequent additions are permitted; 8. The eighth provides a miscellaneous clarification of the characteristics of offenses.
Regarding the first gate, there are five meanings for receiving [the precepts] with the hands.
As the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"First, it is for the purpose of severing the causes and conditions of theft."
Second, to serve as a witness; third, to cease slander;
fourth, to fulfill the qualities of few desires and contentment.
Fifth, it is to give rise to faith and respect in others, thereby enabling non-Buddhists (tīrthika) to obtain benefit;
this is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Following Characteristics" (*Anulakṣaṇa*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
Because the precepts had not yet been established, each individual gave rise to transgressions and faults.
Laypeople rebuked them, saying, "We do not rejoice in seeing such evil persons who wear cut and dyed robes, yet eat food without having received it; this is called taking what is not given."
Next is the oral acceptance by the mind.
This is for the purpose of guarding against physical acceptance; if there were no oral dharma, the object would be lost as soon as it passed from hand to hand.
Because the oral dharma exists, [the object remains] until the limit is reached.
Furthermore, in order to prevent multiple offenses, receiving with the hand prevents only two; this is explained below.
Do the two types of receiving apply to all four kinds of medicine?
Receiving with the hand applies to all four kinds of medicine, because it serves to prevent the appearance of theft.
Receiving by mouth is restricted to three [medicines], excluding the *kālika* (timely) medicine.
There are also cases where receiving by mouth does not permit receiving by hand, being restricted solely to the midday and morning periods.
For the remaining three medicines, receiving by hand is likewise restricted.
If the ritual of "adding the mouth" (*mukha-dhāraṇa*) is performed, it applies to both the proper time (*kāla*) and the improper time (*akāla*).
The *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* states:

The "medicines for the proper time" (*kālabhaiṣajya*) are actually another name for "medicines for the improper time" (*akālabhaiṣajya*). Regarding these three types of medicine—the seven-day medicine and the lifetime medicine—one must have an illness; provided they have not been kept overnight or improperly handled, they may be consumed after receiving them through both hand and mouth.
Regarding the third point, the person to whom the gift is bestowed:
receiving it by hand constitutes five meanings; with the exception of one's own class, it is validly received from the remaining six classes of persons and the three realms of existence.
Receiving it by word applies only to a bhikṣu; for other classes of persons, it is not validly accomplished.
*The Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

In all cases of receiving food, this is done for the purpose of establishing a witness. If one is in a place where there are humans, it does not constitute a valid reception if non-humans, animals, or ignorant children are present;
however, if one is in a place where no humans are present, it is valid even if gods or animals are there.
This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Following Characteristics" regarding the precept against accepting food.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"There are three ways of ceasing from eating: namely, by means of the hand, the mouth, and the eye."

Fourth, the distinctions regarding the formal acceptance of the Dharma (*dharmasamādāna*). Generally speaking, for the acceptance of the Dharma to be valid, the mind and the object must correspond; as stated in the Vinaya, if one mistakenly accepts ghee when it is meant to be oil, the acceptance is not accomplished.
One must receive it with the palms turned upward, as described in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*:
To take [an object] by seizing it from another pure person (śuddhika-pudgala) is contrary to the Dharma;
this is because the mental engagement involves both monastic and lay intentions directed toward the same single object.
Except in cases where one’s vision is impaired, where one has no affinity for śramaṇas, or due to urgent circumstances, one may accept [the object] after it has been placed on the ground.
Since it is already known that many matters regarding these situations conflict with the rules, one should beforehand apply the mind to receive them universally.
This is divided into four parts.

As for the methods of receiving *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines taken at specific times), they are numerous; the corresponding rules (*pratidharma*) are likewise many, as described in detail in the precept on not accepting food and within the section on generating revulsion toward almsgiving.
This merely clarifies the method for the oral administration [of medicine]; the three types of medicine are discussed separately.
First, the non-timely medicine (*vikālabhojana*) is explained.
There are four rules:
There are four factors: first, the medicine received; second, the person who bestows it; third, the recipient; and fourth, the formal method of receiving.
First, the substance of the medicine is clarified.
One who is free from the eight defects may perform the *kavaḍa* (mouthful) rite:

1. Stored overnight; 2. cooked indoors; 3. cooked by oneself; 4. touched by an impure person; 5. five types of leftovers stored overnight; 6. never previously received with one's own hands; 7. having been received, it remains for longer than a brief moment—according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if it is received at an improper time, it may be placed on the ground and set aside; 8. having been received by hand, its original flavor is altered, such as when sweet things turn sour, and so forth.
Second, the person who bestows [the water]:
there are four rules:
first, filter and clarify the color of the water to avoid eating at improper times;
Second, boiling it for the purpose of reheating it later; there is no need to do so if it is to be drunk raw.
Third, sprinkling water to purify it, in order to eliminate any unpleasant odor.
Fourth, the attendant, with a mind of offering, holds it up in his hands and brings it forward.
Third, the recipient:
namely, a bhikṣu who performs three acts:
first, he personally understands the distinctions between the aforementioned liquids, and his intention is identical to that of a person who has been purified.
Second, receiving with palms turned upward constitutes no sign of theft;
third, identifying it by saying "this is for one who eats at the proper time" refers to those who formerly consumed only pure water and required nothing else;
fourth, regarding the formal act of placing food in the mouth, although various schools require its addition, the specific text has not been transmitted, yet the principle is established.
One should go to where the bhikṣu is and, with full decorum, say:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], now for the purpose of treating thirst, have this ginger decoction; because I wish to consume it during the night, I now receive it from the Venerable sir—so stated three times."
"If one simply accepts and drinks it without leaving any remainder, there is no need for it to be prepared according to the formal rules.
In the case of grape juice, pear juice, honey syrup, and so forth, they may be included as "juice" (pāna) according to the specific illness; one merely changes the name of the medicine.
The four rules regarding seven-day medicines are the same as above.
First, clarifying the substance of the medicine itself, it is naturally free from eight defects;
only the eighth is changed: it must not be the seven-day medicine of another bhikṣu, nor medicine remaining after a transgression has been committed.
The remaining seven points are the same as above.
Second, regarding the pure person who may bestow [the food], there are four rules:

first, one must provide it after filtering it; second, it must be distinct from "timely food" (i.e., food to be consumed before noon), such as fat excluding meat, or oil excluding dregs, and so forth.
Second, boiling with fire;
third, purifying with drops of water;
fourth, bestowing with a mind of giving, which the recipient receives with a corresponding mental state.
Regarding the three types of things received by a bhikṣu, there are two [categories].
First, regarding those that one may keep for oneself, provided they are free from five faults: the first is keeping them in continuous succession.
If one keeps [the medicine] until the seventh day, even if it is received on that very day, it does not constitute [a valid possession].

"If a bhikṣu possesses rock honey on the seventh day and on that same day obtains more rock honey, this is called 'contamination' (*saṃsṛṣṭa*)."
Question:

This does not constitute a violation of the rule regarding the "long-term defilement," because once the previous seven-day period has been completed and the illness still does not improve, taking further medicine is of no benefit and the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) cannot be established;
however, if one obtains a different medicinal substance, an additional seven days may be added.
Second, regarding continuous possession:

if one has already been in possession of medicine until the eighth day and commits the offense of *atireka* (excess), and on that very day obtains more medicine which, upon entering one's hand, becomes subject to the rules of formal authorization (*karmavācanā*) and thus becomes tainted, it can no longer be consumed.

Third, if one has previously consumed another's medicine on the seventh day, even if one obtains it oneself on that very day, the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) will not be accomplished because the flavor of the medicine remains connected;

Fourth, receiving for continuous use.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"During the seven-day period, a bhikṣu may receive medicinal substances day by day; having received them, he does not consume them."
Upon reaching the eighth day, one must not receive [the precepts] again; it is necessary to have at least one day’s interval without receiving them.

This is because receiving too many out of greed is a fault, and furthermore, there is no textual authority in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) for taking medicine. Applying this principle is also appropriate.
The five types of continuous offenses.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:

A bhikṣu may take [the medicine] continuously for seven days; on the eighth day, it is permissible only once, after which he may not take more, though this does not prevent him from receiving other medicines.
The above clarifies the continuity [of the procedure], speaking in reference to a single medicinal honey;

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
Raw butter, cooked butter, and clarified butter (ghṛta) change their flavors as they progress, each being received for seven days.
Second, there are four methods of receiving [food] oneself:

Second, regarding the distinction:
it is said that one should maintain the perception that the oil is for seven days.

Third, the acknowledgment of the announcement:
it is unnecessary to say, "In this place pure items have arisen; I shall accept them, provided they are not separated from me and are for a meal at the proper time.

Although they were previously received, because the flavor has changed and the original reception is lost, this is not termed "defiled contact" (*duṣṭa-sparśana*).
The *Vibhāṣā* states: "Once the seven-day medicine has been received by hand and accepted by word, place it in one location and do not let a lay attendant (*karmadāna*) touch it.
Perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) four times."
One should hold the medicine and say:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!

I, the bhikṣu [name], now for the sake of the condition of wind-disease, have this black sesame oil as a seven-day medicine; because I wish to consume it after having kept it overnight for seven days, I now receive it from you, Venerable sir—so stated three times."
"Within this peaceful and pure place, take whatever you require for yourself.

The remaining [medicines] are applied according to their respective antidotes, following the same principles as previously outlined. There are four types of medicines to be taken for the duration of one's life:

Second, the person who bestows it performs three procedures:
first, after purifying it by fire, there is no fault of it returning to its raw state.
Second, it is distinct from other medicines, namely those such as food to be consumed while holding;

The three types of bhikṣus who receive [the medicine] perform three procedures:
1. Receiving with palms upturned: the mental state is the same as that of a pure person (*śuddhaka*).

Regarding the threefold division of the substance: the *ziyuan* (purple yam) pill constitutes the medicinal substance itself, while the sheep kidney serves as a medicinal adjunct;

(Recite this three times.)

Within these pills and powders, according to the specific underlying disease, there are fifty or thirty distinct medicinal colors; each follows its original prescription, with titles and methods of application as distinguished previously.

he should immediately seek out another bhikṣu to hold it for him, and must not exceed the prescribed limit.
Nowadays, those who uphold the Dharma are rare, perhaps only one or two;

Receiving with the hands prevents theft; once one person has received it, it extends to others as well.

The *Aṣṭagrantha-vibhāṣā* clarifies various characteristics.

Question:
Of which offenses do these two restraints of body and speech protect one against? Answer:
Now, the four types of medicine are discussed separately.

For example, regarding *kālabhojana* (medicines taken at the proper time), receiving them with the hand incurs two offenses: the offense of not receiving [them formally] and the offense of improper contact;
the same applies to receiving them orally.

Regarding non-timely liquids (*vikālabhojana*), receiving them with the hands prevents two offenses: first, it prevents the offense of not receiving [the liquid] at all; second, it prevents the offense of grasping it without having received it, which constitutes an improper touch (*duṣṭasparśa*).

Regarding the mouth, it prevents two offenses: first, it prevents the loss of the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) by consuming after midday; second, it prevents the loss of the formal acceptance by consuming after the designated time, which constitutes an improper grasp.
Regarding the seven-day medicine (*saptāha-bhaiṣajya*), one prevents two offenses by receiving it with the hand, as in the case of the *yavāgū*;

one prevents three offenses by mouth: first, preventing the offense of receiving it after the time has passed; second, preventing the offense of improper contact after midday; and third, preventing the offense of storing leftovers overnight. Regarding the phrase "preventing internal storage" mentioned in ancient texts, there is no such scriptural authority here; this is evidenced by the rule for life-long [medicines], which lists [the requirement of] knowing [the time] and does not permit [such storage].
Regarding medicines for as long as one lives, receiving them with the hands is the same as above.
As for guarding against the six offenses through speech:

first, taking after the time has passed; second, not receiving [the medicine]; third, improper contact; fourth, keeping overnight; fifth, cooking inside [the monastery]; sixth, cooking for oneself, because by cooking it transforms the raw into the cooked.
Because offenses arise from not having received [the medicine], there were no transgressions;
now that both types have been received, transgressions arise when the time [for consumption] has passed.
If a seasonal medicine (*kālabhaiṣajya*) is received by hand, two offenses arise during the lapse of time: the forfeiture of the reception and the offense of improper contact (*duṣṭasparśa*).
Overnight, two offenses arise: *saṃstarita* (storing overnight) and *duṣṭasaṃsṛṣṭa* (impure contact).
With non-timely liquids held in the hand, two offenses arise; within simultaneous medicines, three offenses arise when received orally:
*akāla* (non-timely), *saṃstarita*, and *duṣṭasaṃsṛṣṭa*, occurring when the dawn light appears.
Regarding the seven-day medicine, two offenses arise from the hands, as mentioned above;

five offenses arise from speech. When the dawn of the eighth day appears, if one speaks of it, there is the offense of *saṃstuta* (stored overnight), the offense of *vikāla* (improper time), and the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* for forfeiture; furthermore, there is the *pāyattika* for consuming what has been improperly touched, and the *dukkaṭa* for not discarding the medicine. Thus, there are three *thullaccaya*s and two *dukkaṭa*s in full.
Question:
What is meant by "neither arising nor receiving"? Answer:
Since medicine is fundamentally not subject to formal acceptance (*anupasaṃpad*), even if one adds the ritual of verbal declaration, the state of non-acceptance is lost;
when the dawn of the eighth day arrives, there occurs a spontaneous loss of the formal undertaking, which does not mean that one can generate non-acceptance anew.
The *kṣaya-nakṣatra* (residual asterism) is not inherently a residual asterism;
it is because of the existence of the rule regarding the mouth [of the month] that the *kṣaya-nakṣatra* arises on the eighth day.

It is the same with "improper time" (*akāla*): since the substance of the medicine has not yet acquired the status of a formal rule, there is no distinction between proper and improper time; one may accept it for the sake of the illness, and in all such cases, it is permissible.
By means of the ritual of oral administration, the eighth day at dawn is designated as "non-time.

Regarding "for as long as life lasts," receiving [the medicine] with the hands is the same as before; receiving it orally may also result in the commission of six offenses, and taking it when not ill constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The remaining details are clearly explained in the *Anuvyañjana* [Chapter] regarding the three precepts concerning untimely food, food not formally accepted, and food kept overnight.
Question:
Among the four types of medicine, why is the offense for the seven-day medicine more serious, while the other three are lighter?
Answer: First, because it relies on powerful material resources and involves a heavy, defiled state of mind;

second, because while the physical manifestation [of the object] exists constantly and the Noble Ones have declared it to be pure, one instead violates the Buddha’s teachings by failing to acknowledge this transgression—therefore, it is grave.
Other medicines are the opposite of this, and are therefore light.
Question:
When a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, how many offenses does he incur?
Answer: Regarding the medicinal substances to be taken at the proper time, there are seven offenses for each swallow:
taking them at an improper time, consuming leftovers from a previous night, or failing to receive them through formal acceptance—these constitute three *pāyattika* offenses.
There are four *duṣkṛta* offenses: storing food indoors, cooking indoors, cooking for oneself, and receiving food from one who has handled it improperly.
This refers to cases where, after having been kept overnight, one eats it without having formally accepted it or having cooked it oneself;
however, if during the improper time (non-time) a pure person (*pariśuddha-puruṣa*) hands it over, there is no offense for not having formally accepted it.
Other offenses may be judged by this precedent as to their presence or absence.

because they were having a *kappiyakāraka* (an attendant) carry the bowl while begging, an outsider threw medicine into the bowl, and the bhikṣu died. Consequently, the rule was established.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If there is no seat available for washing the bowl, one should squat with the body bent forward, keeping it one span (*vitasti*) above the ground.
One must not use ash, as it will cause the color [of the bowl] to fade."
One should take the juice from tree leaves; "grinding without sand" refers to cow dung.
One must not stand on a precarious bank.
One should first wash the teacher’s bowl and afterwards wash one's own bowl.
One must not pour the residual water from one's own bowl into the teacher's bowl.
Furthermore, having finished washing, one should sit in a squatting posture, take the bowl-sack and its straps, place them over the arm, and hold them upon the knees to contain [the water].
Furthermore, regarding those who wash and dye robes: first provide the teacher’s robes for washing and dyeing;
do not soak your own robes inside the teacher’s robes.

If a bowl has been mended or broken, one must wait until after the meal before untying the mendings, washing it thoroughly, drying it in the sun, and then re-tying it with cord, placing it back in its usual location.
Do not place it on the ground;
even down to a spot where there is nothing, moisten it with water and then set it down securely.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
The almsbowl is the emblem of all Buddhas; it must not be used improperly.
When newly acquired, one should wash the bowl three times with single-minded concentration; this is called purification.
Furthermore, one must not heat it in the midday sun to cause moisture to emerge, for that constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
One should not wash one's hands inside the alms bowl; it should not be used for any purpose whatsoever except in cases of illness.
One should revere it as one does one's own eyes.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"Guard the alms bowl as you would your own eyes.
When washing an iron bowl, it is permitted to hold it one chi above the ground; a ceramic bowl should be held about five or six cun above the ground."
It should be placed in a suitable location.

One must guard this bowl and not place it where tiles or stones might fall upon it; nor should it be leaned against a sword or staff, nor suspended from an object, nor placed in the middle of a path, nor on a stone, nor beneath a fruit tree, nor on uneven ground, nor within a door threshold, nor beneath a door leaf, nor on a rope bed or a wooden bed—except for temporary placement;

If one obtains seven-day medicine, it should be placed within a key-ring, a small bowl, a medium bowl, or a large bowl; it must not be given away as a formal gift (pariṣkāra-dāna), as it is required for the original bowl.

If one suffers from illness due to excessive consumption of food and drink without moderation, one should construct a bathhouse.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
He addressed the fourfold assembly, saying that there are five merits in constructing a bathhouse:
it dispels wind, cures illness, removes dust and grime, makes the body light and agile, and results in a plump and fair complexion.
A bhikṣu should skillfully establish [a bathhouse].

Rubbing one another is also a transgression. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:

In the bathhouse, the senior monk (*sthavira*) should explain to the monks the causes and conditions for bathing; it is not for the sake of adorning the body or for cleanliness, but merely to remove wind and cold from within the body so that one may practice the Path in peace and security.
One should cultivate weariness toward the phenomena of the body and subdue the phenomena of the mind, and should give rise to a heart of loving-kindness.
This is for the purpose of attaining few desires and contentment.

Regarding each of these matters, there are established protocols for the Elder’s delivery of the Dharma; he provides exhortations according to the specific circumstances, which I shall not detail here in full.

This continues until the time of eating, as various needs arise.

*Vinayamātṛkā*: A bhikṣu is permitted to possess only these items: the three robes, the alms bowl, the sitting mat, the needle-case, the water flask, the basin, and so forth.
As for those things he is not permitted to possess: women, gold, silver, all precious objects, all weapons of war, vessels for holding wine, and the like.
Because it gives rise to suspicion among people.

*Ekottarika Āgama*: [as cited above].
To construct a hall and offer it to the Sangha is called an offering to the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* (the Sangha of the four quarters).
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "If a donor builds a hall for a bhikṣu, like a king residing in a palace, all necessary items may be accepted."
When the bhikṣus wished to construct a dwelling, the Buddha instructed them to follow the rules for building dwellings, permitting everything [required] to be provided.
The Vinaya text sets forth every detail exhaustively; I have omitted them here for brevity.
If one receives as an allotment a dilapidated dwelling that cannot be repaired, and refuses to accept it,

The Buddha himself took up wooden tools to repair the temple gate.
Monks are permitted to possess all kinds of tools.
If a monastic dwelling is dilapidated, one may sell a single room to repair another room; likewise, one may sell bedding and utensils to repair them.
Whenever the communal hall or a private room falls into disrepair, the presiding elder (upādhyāya) or the resident elder should personally perform the preliminary manual labor.
Kāśyapa repeatedly trod the mud to plaster the monks' quarters, and so forth.
A bhikṣu may build a dwelling for himself using timber.

When a bhikṣu constructs a dwelling and wishes to plaster the walls and decorate them with the five colors, he may do so;
however, images depicting the union of men and women must be excluded. All other subjects, such as mountains, forests, people, and horses, are permitted.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "It must not be used [for this purpose].
It should not be adorned with embroidery or brocade; however, it is permitted to use those with various other colors or patterns of birds and beasts."
If Ānanda obtains a separate room, he may open it and accept it.
If a private room is constructed upon communal monastic land, one must rise when a guest arrives;
if one does not rise, the room must be returned to the communal land, for it is improper to incorporate communal land into one's own possession.
If one constructs a dwelling, it shall not be completed abruptly, as it would otherwise lack solidity;
if one builds a large multi-storied hall, a period of twelve years for its construction is permitted;
for other structures, the scale and duration shall be determined according to their size and requirements.

If a *karmadāna* bhikṣu has completed the construction of a dwelling that is well-adorned, perfumed with incense, and fully equipped with all necessities, he shall reside in that dwelling and move from it only once every ninety days; he must not accept another dwelling.
If there is a layperson who can repair a dilapidated room, it should be granted to them through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one announcement).

if one offers it to the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha and then gives it to the Saṃgha, it is likewise."
If there are donors for the dwellings and bedding, one may only look after them; one must not take one thing away to give another.
For one who repairs a dilapidated dwelling, they may reside there for six years;
for one who builds a new dwelling, they may reside there for twelve years.

Previously, when a monastic dwelling was dilapidated and its doors and windows were reoriented, after two or three years—according to the amount of labor expended—the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) was performed to grant [the resident] the right to stay.

Chapter Twenty: On Cultivating Merit through Giving (Part Two). Now, merit arises from the field of purity, and the Way originates in few desires.
For a family that performs meritorious deeds, the offerings should be as weighty and abundant as possible;
for those who receive the gifts, they should be as modest and frugal as possible.
To provide much without weariness is the way of merit.
To receive only a small, limited amount is the proper conduct for one who practices through faith.
As the Vinaya states:
"Though a donor may give without weariness, the recipient should know contentment!"
However, those who have left the household life wear the robes of the sages;
this dependent form requires material support to be established.
If one does not accept offerings at the time they are given, it will be difficult to obtain them later.
If one is skillfully responsive to the principles of the Dharma, there will be no flaw between the subject and the object;
yet if one does not necessarily rely on external affairs, upon what could the standard for practice be based?

If one can skillfully reflect when resources are meager and remain capable yet free from worldly entanglements, this is what is meant by the establishment of the conditions for the Way; thus, practice arises from this.
Why is this? Greed arises from emotional attachment; freedom from defilement results from self-restraint.
To indulge the mind leads to delusion through the pursuit of flavors, whereas to fix one's resolve leads even to fine delicacies producing a sense of revulsion.
Thus, good and evil arise from within the heart, while one's ascent or descent depends upon the space of a single square inch.
For this reason, those who practice the Way should not allow themselves to be heedless or unrestrained;
they must not disregard the conditions of time, allowing affairs to become stagnant, nor fail to exercise moderation, thereby escaping the deep net [of suffering]. Is this not tragic!
Yet craving is difficult to satisfy, like the ocean swallowing rivers;
if one restrains it with the Dharma, all afflictions will be stilled.
Since you have already distinguished your outward form and attire from those of the world, your aspirations are marked by their loftiness and greatness.
How could such defiled traces be tolerated within the realm of worldly affairs?
Even those of the nine schools of secular thought still hold food and clothing in contempt;
yet you, who have cast yourselves into the noble lineage of the Triple Gem, remain mired in the initial steps of your practice and are about to fall back into the mire. How lamentable this is!
Now, I shall briefly describe this process through gradual stages and cite authentic texts below, so that those who cherish the Way may examine them closely and restrain their conduct accordingly.

This is divided into five parts: first, clarifying the person who receives the offering; second, clarifying the expedient means for wearying oneself of and treating [defilements]; third, clarifying the teachings on establishing contemplation; fourth, clarifying the methods for performing contemplation; and fifth, clarifying the various signs encountered during the course of treatment.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of this topic], the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
There are four ways in which a bhikṣu may consume donated goods;
the first is "theft-like consumption."
If a bhikṣu accepts offerings while violating the precepts, it is called "using through theft.
Second is "using as a debtor":
at the time of receiving an offering, one must form this thought; if one does not, one incurs guilt, for one becomes a debtor to the faithful offerings of others.
Third is the use by close friends, which refers to the seven types of trainees (*śaikṣa*) receiving offerings.
Fourth is the use by the master, which refers to the Arhat.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:

Because those who receive the faithful offerings of others but fail to use them according to the Dharma, allowing their minds to become negligent and abandoning their practice of the Path, will enter the three miserable realms to undergo heavy suffering.

If they were not to undergo this retribution of suffering, then upon eating the food offered by others' faith, it would immediately break through their bellies and come out; and upon wearing the clothing, it would immediately detach from their bodies.
If one knows that the recipient has no merit (karma) yet still bestows a gift, both the giver and the recipient fall into the category of those who have failed in their giving.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies this through four permutations: the giver is pure while the recipient is impure, and so forth.
If a renunciant lacks both precepts and wisdom yet consumes the offerings of the faithful, they will enter the Hell of Copper Stakes and undergo the two sufferings of iron pellets and iron broth.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:

"Even for offenses as minor as a *duṣkṛta*, if one accepts offerings from others or receives the prostrations and respect of a precept-keeping bhikṣu without a valid reason, it is not permissible to accept them."
Second, the clarification of the skillful means for cultivation through revulsion. As stated in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*:
"How does a bhikṣu contemplate the robes he wears and cultivate the perception of non-delight?"
Whether sewing clothes, seeing clothes, touching clothes, wearing clothes, or taking off clothes;
when observing them at such times as being like blood-stained skin— putrid, foul-smelling, loathsome, and an abode for insects— when one observes in this way,
the greedy mind toward clothes is immediately extinguished.
How does one cultivate the perception of the repulsiveness of food?
If a bhikṣu holds his alms bowl, he should regard it as being like a skull smeared with blood—putrid, foul-smelling, loathsome, and a dwelling place for insects;
and when he receives food, he should contemplate that this food is like a corpse-insect.

If one sees flour, one should conceive of it as powdered bone; when receiving rice gruel, one should conceive of it as excrement broth; when receiving various cakes, one should conceive of them as human skin; the alms-bowl staff one holds should be conceived of as human bone; when receiving milk or curd, one should conceive of them as thick blood and sweat; and if one receives vegetables, one should conceive of them as hair and body hair;
when receiving various kinds of drinks, one should conceive of them as blood. This is called generating the perception of non-delight regarding food.
What is the perception of dissatisfaction regarding dwellings?
When entering a dwelling, one should reflect upon it as being like a hell where various sufferings and afflictions are experienced;
such a dwelling is merely a composite of all its constituent parts.
The timber is the human bones, and the earth is the human flesh; even all beds, couches, quilts, and bedding are likewise so.
When one contemplates in this manner, it is called the perception of the world as being unlovely.
If one can contemplate such perceptions as these, that person will immediately attain the Dharma as it truly is.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
